claims.title: Snip internal URL shortener backend
claims.body: Build Snip, an internal URL shortener for the company used by marketing and the docs team. Must create short links, redirect fast, and later track click analytics.

claims.title: PostgreSQL is the source of truth
claims.body: Standardize on PostgreSQL as the primary datastore. A Redis read cache may be added later if reads get hot, but Postgres remains source of truth. Settled — do not reopen.

claims.title: Random 7-char base62 short codes
claims.body: Short codes are random, 7 characters, base62 — exactly. Chosen over sequential ids to prevent enumeration. Format is externally committed: marketing printed it and a partner contract references '7-character Snip codes'. Frozen.

claims.title: Unique constraint + retry on collision
claims.body: Handle random-code collisions with a unique constraint on the code column plus generate-check-retry on insert.

claims.title: 302 redirect via single indexed code lookup
claims.body: Redirect resolves via a single indexed lookup on the code column. Use HTTP 302 (not 301) to enable analytics interception later.

claims.title: Click tracking must not slow redirects
claims.body: Every redirect records a click event (timestamp, referrer, coarse geo) without slowing the redirect. The write path must be fire-and-forget/async.

claims.title: DynamoDB/Redis as source of truth
claims.body: AI proposed DynamoDB or Redis as the primary datastore.
claims.reason: Standardizing on PostgreSQL which ops knows well; at expected volume a KV store is unwanted overhead. Redis allowed only as an optional later read cache, not source of truth.

claims.title: Auto-increment ids exposed in URLs
claims.body: AI proposed exposing the row's auto-increment id in the URL.
claims.reason: Sequential ids are enumerable (walk /1,/2,/3 to scrape every link) and leak link counts. Rejected in favor of random 7-char base62.

claims.title: How to reserve/arbitrate vanity codes
claims.body: Custom vanity URLs collide with the random code space; no decision yet on how to reserve or arbitrate them. Parked.

claims.title: Click analytics milestone
claims.body: Storage and redirect are done and deployed. Current milestone is click analytics.

claims.title: Build async click-tracking write path
claims.body: Build the click-tracking write path as fire-and-forget so redirects stay fast.

claims.title: Emit click events to application logs / CloudWatch
claims.body: Week 7 idea: emit each click event to application logs / CloudWatch and parse into reports later.

claims.title: Store click events in a clicks table in main Postgres
claims.body: Week 7 decision after scrapping the logs idea: store click events in a `clicks` table in the primary Postgres, next to the links.

claims.title: Analytics goes into a separate ClickHouse store; Postgres serves links only
claims.body: Week 8 current decision: all click events go to a SEPARATE analytics store (ClickHouse) via the async write path. The primary Postgres serves ONLY links. Replaces both the logs idea and the clicks-in-main-Postgres plan.

claims.reason: Logs/CloudWatch are hard to query for real analytics and retention gets expensive; superseded by the dedicated ClickHouse analytics store.

Load testing showed analytics inserts at real click volume bloat the primary Postgres and contend with link-serving reads, slowing redirects and violating the 'redirects must stay fast' rule; superseded by moving analytics to a separate ClickHouse store.

claims.title: Build async click-tracking write path shipping events to ClickHouse
claims.body: Build the async click-tracking write path that ships click events to ClickHouse without slowing the redirect.

claims.reason: The write path's target store changed from the main Postgres clicks table to the separate ClickHouse analytics store following the Week 8 decision.

claims.title: Use 301 permanent redirects for share links
claims.body: Switch public share-link redirects from 302 to 301 permanent so browsers and CDNs cache them and marketing gains SEO link equity. The 302 was originally kept as an analytics interception hook, but analytics now runs async to ClickHouse, so the hook is no longer needed.

claims.title: Support 8-character codes for campaign namespace
claims.body: Add a 'campaign codes' namespace for human-readable-ish codes used in big marketing pushes. To avoid collisions with the existing code space, campaign codes are allowed to be 8 characters.

claims.reason: [AUTO-RECONCILED] 302's sole justification was analytics interception; analytics now runs async to ClickHouse, so 301 permanent redirects (browser/CDN caching + SEO) supersede it.

claims.note: New 8-char campaign codes clash with the FROZEN 7-char base62 format, which is externally committed (marketing + partner contract referencing '7-character Snip codes'). Cannot be auto-adopted. Whether a separate campaign namespace is exempt from the contractual 7-char guarantee is a human decision. New claim parked; frozen claim untouched.

claims.title: Move primary link store to DynamoDB global tables
claims.body: New requirement: sub-50ms redirects worldwide. Move the primary source of truth for links from single-region Postgres to DynamoDB global tables for multi-region low-latency reads.

claims.reason: New hard requirement for global sub-50ms redirects made single-region Postgres insufficient as the primary store; moved to DynamoDB global tables.
